description: Hardware Hacking Village at DEF CON 26 covers hands-on hardware security and reverse engineering with 5 talks on NFC payments, RF hacking, WiFi exploitation, drone building, firmware analysis, and retro computing.

talks.title: NFC Payments The Art of Relay & Replay
talks.teaser: NFC Payments The Art of Relay & Replay
talks.summary:
### Exploiting Near-Field Communication Payment Systems
At 00:00, hardware security researcher Salvador Mendoza presents offensive research targeting Near-Field Communication (NFC) payment architectures, demonstrating practical relay and replay attacks against mobile wallets and contactless cards.

### Mobile Payment Tokenization Mechanics
At 05:01, Mendoza analyzes the tokenization process used by mobile payment platforms (such as Apple Pay and Samsung Pay). While mobile systems avoid transmitting primary account numbers (PANs) by generating dynamic cryptograms and transient tokens, underlying protocol flaws can leave these tokens vulnerable to manipulation.

### Replay Vulnerabilities and Token Lifetime Exploitation
At 10:02, the speaker demonstrates replay attack vectors. Mendoza exposes timing flaws where payment tokens remain valid across multiple transaction windows or can be pre-computed, harvested wirelessly, and replayed hours later at unattended Point of Sale (PoS) terminals.

### Custom Hardware Prototyping and Miniaturization
At 15:00, Mendoza showcases custom offensive hardware designs. Utilizing SPI/I2C communication modules, ultra-thin inductive coils, and microcontrollers, he demonstrates building miniature interception devices that fit covertly into standard payment reader bezels or smartphone cases.

### Real-Time Wireless Relay Attacks and Defensive Mitigations
Concluding between 20:02 and 25:01, the presentation explores real-time relay attacks. By streaming harvested NFC transaction frames over long-distance Wi-Fi or cellular connections to a proxy device at a remote payment terminal, an attacker can charge a victim's card in real time. Mendoza concludes by recommending strict PoS response timeouts and geofenced transaction limits to defeat relay techniques.

talks.title: Hacking your HackRF
talks.summary:
### Architecture of the HackRF One Platform
At 00:00, Mike Davis presents an in-depth hardware and firmware hacking guide for the HackRF One software-defined radio (SDR) at the Hardware Hacking Village. Davis reviews the core components of the HackRF, including the LPC43xx ARM Cortex-M4/M0 dual-core microcontroller, MAX2837 transceiver, and CPLD logic.

### Direct Memory Access and Microcontroller Offloading
At 03:50 and 07:35, Davis explains how the HackRF processes high-speed RF samples. By offloading baseband sample streaming entirely to Direct Memory Access (DMA) channels and the CPLD, the main ARM processor core remains largely idle during standard transmission and reception.

### Writing Custom On-Device Signal Processing Routines
At 12:00, the speaker details how developers can customize the HackRF firmware. By taking advantage of idle MCU cycles in the main firmware loop, developers can implement on-device packet decoding, frequency hopping, and trigger logic directly in firmware, eliminating the latency of streaming raw I/Q samples over USB to a host PC.

### External Clock Synchronization and Multi-Device Arrays
Concluding between 15:59 and 18:00, Davis demonstrates the use of the external clock input and output ports on the HackRF. By sharing a common clock source across multiple HackRF boards, researchers can synchronize sampling clocks to build coherent multi-antenna SDR arrays for radio direction finding and beamforming.

talks.title: The Cactus 6502 Blinkenlights 40 Years Late
talks.summary:
### Recreating the Era of Processor Front-Panel Blinkenlights
At 00:00, Commodore Z presents "The Cactus 6502," a custom hardware engineering project that resurrects physical front-panel indicator lamps and manual single-stepping for the classic MOS Technology 6502 microprocessor.

### The 1977 Watershed: From Front Panels to Appliance Computers
At 10:04, Commodore Z chronicles computing history, identifying 1977 as the pivotal year when self-contained "appliance computers" (such as the Apple II, Commodore PET, and TRS-80) eclipsed early hobbyist systems like the Altair 8800 and IMSAI 8080. While integrated displays and keyboards democratized computing, they hid internal bus states from direct user view.

### Address Control Card and DMA Hardware Architecture
At 20:01, the speaker details the system architecture of The Cactus. He explains the design of the address control card, which intercepts processor address lines, synchronizes bus cycles, and executes Direct Memory Access (DMA) routines to read and write memory without host CPU intervention.

### Discrete Logic Design: Counters, Flip-Flops, and Cycle Trapping
At 30:00, the presentation explores the low-level circuit design. Using cascading ripple counters, discrete flip-flop arrays, and clock generator circuits, The Cactus can halt the 6502 processor mid-instruction, trap machine states, and display bus contents across rows of physical LEDs.

### Pedagogical Value of Hardware-Level Visibility
Concluding between 40:00 and 50:00, Commodore Z highlights the educational power of physical blinkenlights. Manually clocking a microprocessor step-by-step through fetch, decode, and execute cycles provides software engineers and retrocomputing enthusiasts with an intuitive understanding of computer architecture.
